articles.headline: Nvidia’s latest GPU driver brings a new way to speed up PC games
keyFacts: Nvidia is releasing the 621.01 GPU driver to enable Microsoft's Advanced Shader Delivery technology for faster game launches.
The technology uses cloud compilation to eliminate mid-game shader compilation, reducing CPU spikes and stuttering in supported games.
Gears of War: E-Day and Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 currently support the new system through the Xbox PC app.
body: Nvidia is rolling out a new GPU driver today (621.01) that enables Microsoft’s new Advanced Shader Delivery technology to speed up game launches. The technology also removes mid-game “just-in-time” shader compilation, reducing stuttering and CPU spikes.
Nvidia’s latest GPU driver brings a new way to speed up PC games
Microsoft’s new Advanced Shader Delivery technology is now part of Nvidia’s drivers.

Microsoft’s Advanced Shader Delivery works by offloading shader compilation for different hardware combinations to the cloud. “Using DirectX 12, Windows 11, and the Microsoft Agility SDK, developers capture shaders into a State Object Database (SODB), allowing Microsoft’s cloud network to precompile shaders for hundreds of thousands of hardware and driver combinations,” explains Nvidia’s Andrew Burnes.

Gears of War: E-Day and Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 now both support Advanced Shader Delivery, as long as you download the games via the Xbox PC app. “This system is storefront-agnostic, meaning you benefit even when playing games purchased on Steam, as long as the Xbox PC app is installed on your PC,” says Burnes.

Advanced Shader Delivery will let you skip the annoying shader compilation screen in Call of Duty, and it should improve the overall performance of supported games. “With a near-100 percent cache hit rate, it eliminates mid-game ‘just-in-time’ shader compilation, wiping out CPU spikes and frame stutters in titles like Gears of War: E-Day, and Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.

You can download Nvidia’s latest 621.01 update here, and Advanced Shader Delivery is also supported on AMD GPUs with Adrenalin 26.6.1 or higher and Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 series with driver version 2026.08.3 or higher.

articles.headline: Three reasons why the Brewers can finally win their first World Series title
keyFacts: The Milwaukee Brewers reached the World Series for the first time since 1982 and entered as favorites against the Tampa Bay Rays.
The Brewers ranked second in Major League Baseball in regular-season scoring and batting average, relying on a well-rounded offense.
The Brewers finished the regular season with a league-best 103-59 record and maintained a 7-1 record in the playoffs.
body: The Milwaukee Brewers have made the World Series for the first time since 1982 and enter the series as the favorite against the Tampa Bay Rays. One of the most fun aspects of the series is that both teams are vying for their first-ever World Series title.

While the Rays, in their 29th season of existence, have played in the World Series twice since 2008, the Brewers are in the Fall Classic for just the second time in franchise history and the first since joining the National League in 1998.
Why could this finally be the year for the Brewers (other than that they're awesome)? Let's dive in with the three biggest reasons.
1. A well-rounded offense
The Brewers scored the second-most runs in baseball in 2026, getting them home in numerous ways
At 832 runs in 162 games (5.14 runs per game), the Brewers ranked second in the majors in the regular season in scoring. How'd they get there? In any way you can imagine.

The Brewers were first in batting average (.258) and on-base percentage (.341), which is a killer combination. Though they didn't rank highly in home runs (154, tied for 28th), they were fifth in doubles (279) and sixth in triples (26). They flash speed on the bases, sitting fifth in stolen bases (162). You'll hear plenty in this series about "small ball" (mostly because the two teams are known as small-market ballclubs and it's a convenient talking point) and the Brewers were fifth in sac bunts (37).
The Brewers are a "little things" team. They don't beat themselves and find ways to excel on the margins. In addition to the bunting and base-stealing, they rarely hit into double plays.

Also, there's been plenty of talk about the lack of home runs, and it's true that the Brewers finished tied for 28th in homers as a team this season. That doesn't mean there's a total void of power. Some of the issues were early in the season. The Brewers slugged .430 in September, compared to .398 before the All-Star break.

William Contreras has more power potential than shown by the 18 home runs he hit during the season. Jake Bauers emerged with 26 homers and had a huge blast in the last round. Brice Turang isn't a traditional power hitter, but he hit 21 in the regular season. Jackson Chourio missed time with an injury but still hit 25 in his 127 games. Remember, he's only 22 years old, too.
The Brewers have hit 10 home runs in their seven playoff games thus far, including some absolute monster blasts, timing-wise.
Probably the best way to phrase it is that the Brewers can hit home runs, but they just don't rely on it. They are well-rounded.
2. Excellent run prevention
High-end starters, an excellent bullpen and stellar defense? Milwaukee has it all
Behind probable Cy Young winner Jacob Misiorowski and emerging frontline starter Logan Henderson, the Brewers sported a great rotation in 2026. The bullpen is outstanding, too.

In the regular season, the Brewers' team ERA was 3.51, the second-lowest in baseball. They miss bats, sitting second in strikeouts (1544), and also do a nice job of keeping guys off base, as they were fourth in WHIP (1.18).

When the ball is put in play, Brewers pitchers can trust their defense. Only six teams committed fewer errors. Range is plenty important, too, and the Brewers rate highly nearly all over the diamond. They were fifth in outs above average, which accounts for range in its calculation. Defensive efficiency measures the percentage of balls put into play that are converted into outs. The Brewers were sixth there at .712.
Turang and Chourio are the stars here, but it's a great group as a whole.
And that bullpen can be killer. You'll see contributions from the likes of DL Hall, JoJo Romero and others, but especially from the big guns:
- Aaron Ashby can cover multiple innings. He had 116 strikeouts in 89 ⅓ regular-season innings. So far in the playoffs? Ridiculous. He hasn't allowed a run in 12 ⅓ innings of work.
- Abner Uribe has nasty stuff and showed it with a 1.97 ERA in the regular season. He's had one rough postseason outing, but that was an outlier.
- Trevor Megill was one of baseball's best closers this season and has five scoreless playoff outings.
3. They're the best team
After 103 regular-season wins, the Brewers are 7-1 in the playoffs

Sure, it's obvious, but it's true. The Brewers had the best record in baseball in the regular season at 103-59. They had the best run differential at +214 (the Rays were at +86 with a 98-64 record). The Brewers have gone 7-1 so far in the playoffs, too, and are now 110-60 this season. They started 13-13 and then were "only" 18-16. Since then, they've just gone absolutely bonkers with winning.
They're exceptional at home (59-26 with the playoffs included) and still pretty great on the road (51-34, playoffs included).

The best team doesn't always win in a seven-game series in a sport that has a 162-game marathon of a regular season. We saw the playoff team with the worst record win it all in 2021 and a 90-win team take the title two years later. Still, generally speaking, being the best team is a pretty good formula to win.
The Brewers have been the best team in baseball since early May.

articles.headline: How to spot a white label gadget, and why that's important
keyFacts: White label gadgets are mass-produced by a single factory and sold under multiple different brand names by various companies.
Engadget noted that consumers can spot white label products by checking for identical promotional images, identical specifications, and shared companion apps.
Engadget advised consumers to research products thoroughly online and check for independent reviews before making a purchase.
body: How to spot a white label gadget, and why that's important
Forewarned is forearmed, after all.

A few weeks ago, the Engadget team was swapping war stories about covering tech in the face of an ever-growing glut of white label devices. Tech, pumped out by a single factory, then sold on to others who put their name on it to sell. They're often attached to a Zombie Brand, as it's an easy way to sell mediocre tech to an unsuspecting public. That's not to say white label tech is bad per se, but it helps to know what you're buying before you hand your money over. So I've sketched out this brief spotter's guide to make sure you're not going to get duped.
White labels 101

Device manufacturing is the province of a small cluster of Asian factories. Very few companies actually make their own hardware. Even those with a long history of designing and building products outsource the actual work this way. White label manufacturing is a legitimate practice, and even big names will add their brand to gear made by their ostensible rivals. Take Sony, which put its name on Samsung and LG-made panels years before it sold its TV business to TCL.

But there are also plenty of generic, sometimes copycat devices, stamped out by an Original Device Manufacturer (ODM). In one example, Engadget's camera guru Steve Dent found the exact same gimbal camera available under three different names. Ordro's UHD-M5, AgfaPhoto Realimove MC3X and Minolta Showtime MN5KG100 even have identical pictures on their Amazon listings. And it's not just camera gear that is rife with products like this.

I was examining the broader smart ring market and found a whole heap of branded rings which could be traced back to a single ODM, J-Style. On its website, J-Style says it offers a rapid white label service for its rings, including custom packaging and logo placement. And it appears the rings offered by Fittr, Qalo and Insix all use the same J-Style X1 under different names. On a similar note, the Reebok/F50 smart ring, which is sold by The Original Fit Factory, looks awfully similar to J-Style's X6 ring.
How to spot a white label

You already know the easiest and smartest thing to do before buying any product is look it up on the internet. I'd advise skipping the AI overview in favor of actual reviews both from sites like this one, and on social media platforms like Reddit. If something's not very good, or comes from a brand with a less than stellar reputation, it's going to be hard to keep that fact quiet for long. If there are no reviews beyond customer recommendations on the product page, it's a sign the company is looking to avoid the scrutiny that comes from being independently reviewed.
Brand

The biggest names in the technology industry have taken a lot of time and effort to build trust with the public. If the name is particularly weighty, the less likely they are to risk it with a low-effort product produced by an unnamed third party. Oftentimes, it's the medium-sized company that's happier to license the brand to third parties for products outside their usual domain.

A good example here is Reebok, a company known for making footwear and apparel and apparel-related things. But you can also buy Reebok-branded exercise equipment (RFE International), Reebok-branded eyewear (Mondottica), a Reebok-branded smart ring (The Original Fit Factory), Reebok-branded smart glasses (by Lucyd) and a Reebok-branded smartwatch (CE Brands/Vitalist).

Similarly, a formerly notable tech giant like Motorola, which is now Lenovo's mobile brand, is happy to license its name. The company ceased making its own wearables nearly a decade ago, and its watches since then were made by licensees. This can wind up backfiring and hurting the brand if the product sold under the name isn't very good. I can only speak to my time with the 2026 Moto Watch (also by CE Brands/Vitalist).

At the bottom of the pile are the Zombie Brands, names from a few years back which have been picked up for pennies at a bankruptcy auction. These are snapped up by various ODMs or their partners for a memorable name to slap on an otherwise cheap product. One of the most notable must be Kodak, which has had its brand sliced and shared out among so many companies it's hard to keep track.
Track record and the pitch

A crucial benefit of the white label process, for both new companies and zombie brands, is that it's an easy way to enter a new market. If you're a company looking to enter the gadget space, harnessing an ODM is a quick and easy way to do so without a lot of risk. At least, not to them, since most of the risk is taken on by the consumer parting with cash for the product.

That's a useful tell for wary customers, since if your local bakery suddenly starts selling smart glasses, you can probably guess they didn't make it. If a company enters a space it's had no experience in, and they don't spend a lot of time talking about the product, it's a white label. Sure, it's not unheard of that an analog company would enter the tech space, but they'll also be more than willing to spend hours talking about it.

In fact, that's true for most tech companies, since they sure love to talk about the process which led to the product's creation. Even for the most mundane devices, they'll wheel a designer out to wax lyrical about the improvements they've made to the product.
Amazon

If you're worried the gadget you're looking to buy could be from a white label, it's often good to look on Amazon. As part of the whole "low cost, low effort" nature of these devices, you'll often find the same device sold under multiple names by multiple brands. Often, they'll be marketed using the same set of images supplied by the ODM, resulting in a scroll of products which all look the same. Or it's the same initial render with the odd tweak, because one company has their own pricey Photoshop subscription.

For instance, let's take a look at the low-end fitness tracker market where Xiaomi's various bands reign supreme. Scroll past the name brand options, however, and you'll soon find a series of listings that look very similar indeed. YJYK, Nhemeylp, Spurkey, Moremore and Flywin all use the same promotional image of their fitness trackers. The only difference is the use of a slightly different watch face, some better edited onto the render than others.

Second, of course, is the fact the specs aren't just very similar, they're identical to one another. All of them are fitness trackers with 1.1-inch AMOLED touchscreens, 25 sport modes and the same sensor functions. An even bigger tell is that they all use the same Keep Health companion app, no matter which company is selling them. Which, if nothing else, means you can look at all of the various listings and pick up the cheapest one knowing the product will be the same.
Caveat emptor

Again, this isn't to denounce any and all white label gadgets as inherently bad, or not worth your time. It's more that, as everything gets pricier, those suspiciously-cheap devices on the second and third pages of your Amazon search can look a lot more tempting. We've all been bitten by those temptations, and normally the only thing we've lost is the time it takes to request a refund. But if you can avoid that issue, surely you'd do so anyway.

articles.headline: AI 'antidetect' browsers are making scams, fraud, and influence operations harder to spot
keyFacts: Security researchers from Check Point Research reported that cybercriminals are using antidetect browsers with stolen session cookies to evade fraud detection and hijack accounts.
Researchers stated that Russian, Iranian, and Chinese hackers are using these tools along with artificial intelligence automation to scale scams, loan fraud, and fake accounts.
Researchers advised security teams and companies to update their detection systems to focus on browser fingerprint inconsistencies and unusual session-cookie patterns.
body: - Cybercriminals use antidetect browsers to disguise devices, hijack accounts, and evade fraud detection systems
- Stolen session cookies, fake identities, and AI automation help scale scams and account abuse
- Researchers warn AI-integrated antidetect tools are lowering barriers for large-scale fraud operations

Cybercriminals have started using antidetect browsers as part of their tech stack, helping them evade detection while deploying session cookies, creating thousands of fake accounts, and passing Know Your Customer (KYC) checks. This is according to a new in-depth report published by security experts Check Point Research (CPR), in which it says that Russian, Iranian, and Chinese hackers are spearheading these activities.
What are antidetect browsers?

When users log into services like Facebook or TikTok using regular browsers, they leave behind digital fingerprints - screen resolution, operating system, fonts. This information can be used to identify and track a device across online sessions, and if a single entity (for example, a digital marketing agency) tries logging into multiple accounts from the same browser, it might trigger a security alert (or simply go against certain terms of service).

Hence the need for antidetect browsers - specialized software whose key feature is the ability to create isolated profiles with different digital fingerprints, making multiple accounts appear to originate from separate devices.
They are generally used to manage social media accounts, advertising, and e-commerce accounts, or to run web scraping operations or test websites across environments.

Antidetect browsers are not malicious by design, and are mostly used by digital marketing agencies and affiliate marketers. However, just as many other good things, these browsers are actively used by cybercriminals to exploit the tech and run fraudulent accounts.
Many competing tools are available today, but a handful stand out - Kameleo, AdsPower, Multilogin, GoLogin, and Dolphin Anty.

According to CPR, underground forums are full of discussions on using antidetect browsers for different fraudulent activities. These mostly originate from Chinese, Iranian, or Russian hackers, and generally revolve around Kameleo, AdsPower, and Multilogin.

“We selected these specifically on the basis of documented references across underground forums and criminal marketplaces, indicating active adoption beyond their stated commercial purposes,” CPR explained.

Analyzing these discussions, CPR discovered that the threat actors primarily use antidetect browsers to leverage stolen session cookies. When they steal a cookie, they can inject it into a clean browser profile to assume control of the account and operate it unabated. Banking accounts and cryptocurrency wallets are the most popular targets.
AI seasoning

Besides banks and crypto wallets, threat actors are also using these browsers to test payment credentials across e-commerce platforms without triggering any alarms. They’re also using them to apply for loans under fabricated identities, and to create fake accounts in bulk, which are then used to generate advertising revenue at scale.

At the same time, Artificial Intelligence is making these operations easier to scale, CPR says. AdsPower, for example, offers integration with Large Language Models (LLM) through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, allowing AI-powered workflows to connect with browser profiles. Through automation marketplaces, it also offers different templates for things like commenting, liking, or sending messages across multiple accounts.

A combination of antidetect browsers, AI account management, and AI generated content creates a powerful concoction that allows threat actors to run large, coordinated campaigns with minimal involvement. This allows them to build and “warm up” fake accounts over time, which then appear more credible and are easier to use in scam and fraud attacks.

“The antidetect browser ecosystem represents a sophisticated, commercially mature, and increasingly AI-driven infrastructure that has fundamentally lowered the barrier to running scam and fraud operations, as well as coordinated inauthentic operations at scale,” CPR warns. “These commercially maintained tools are available in dozens of languages, backed by customer support teams, tested daily against the world’s largest social media platforms, and are now integrated with LLM pipelines that remove the human operator from the execution layer.”

The researchers advise security teams to look beyond account behavior and focus on the infrastructure, including residential proxies, browser fingerprint inconsistencies, and unusual session-cookie patterns. Social media platforms should start analyzing antidetect browsers to better understand how they bypass their detection mechanisms, while companies should review whether their security systems can detect account takeovers involving session cookies.

articles.headline: Kildunne drops to bench as England ring changes
keyFacts: England head coach John Mitchell dropped star full-back Ellie Kildunne to the bench after the team lost 24-21 to Canada, ending a 41-match unbeaten streak.
Mitchell stated that his side lost control and hunger during the defeat, emphasizing the need to fix their performance and accountability.
Emma Sing, Helena Rowland, Mia Venner, and Sadia Kabeya join the starting line-up for Saturday's rematch against Canada in Ottawa.
body: - Published
Star full-back Ellie Kildunne has been dropped to the bench as England shake up their selection in response to a first defeat in four years.
Kildunne was part of the starting XV who lost 24-21 to Canada last Friday in Toronto with the Red Roses' unbeaten streak ending at 41 matches.
Head coach John Mitchell has accused his side of losing the hunger that fuelled a run which took in four successive Six Nations Grand Slams and last year's landmark world title on home soil.
"Last Friday, we lost sight of what we could control when it mattered most. That's on us to fix," said Mitchell.
"This week is about getting back to who we are - hungry, accountable to each other and demanding more of ourselves than anyone outside this group ever could."

Emma Sing comes in at full-back in Kildunne's place for Saturday's rematch (00:00 BST) against Canada in Ottawa, while Tatyana Heard and Claudia Moloney-MacDonald - backline starters in the defeat - drop out of the matchday squad entirely.
Helena Rowland and Mia Venner replace Heard and Moloney-MacDonald at inside centre and wing respectively.

In the fourth change to the starting line-up, Sadia Kabeya, who appeared off the bench last week on her comeback from a leg injury, starts with Alex Matthews, two-time Rugby World Cup winner, dropping to the bench.
Exeter's Flo Robinson and Sale's Hollie Aitchison are included on the bench as a new-look set of half-back replacements.
Sing, a rangy runner who can also kick goals, started two matches at full-back during England's Six Nations campaign, with Kildunne switching to a different position on the wing on each occasion.
Sing's Gloucester-Hartpury team-mate Venner made her England debut in 2020 aged just 17.
Venner has won only another four caps since but was putting pressure on England's more established back three at the start of this year, appearing in wins over Scotland and Italy.
The 24-year-old finished as the PWR's joint top try-scorer last season, crossing 12 times.
Moloney-MacDonald cost her side an early try in the defeat by Canada when, after doing superbly to pick Jess Breach's pass off her toes, she spilled the ball over the line in the sixth minute.
"We've earned a strong period but nothing about it is owed to us going forward," said Mitchell.
"Friday [Saturday 00:00 BST] is an opportunity to apply sustained pressure, learn from what we missed and come out the other side better than we went in."

articles.headline: Cristiano Ronaldo asked for punishment ‘without mitigation’, then fought to cut it
keyFacts: Cristiano Ronaldo successfully had his suspension and fine halved after arguing his clean disciplinary record and his past services to football.
Ronaldo left a Portugal training camp in Denmark without prior justification last month after telling the federation president he was not in the right frame of mind.
It remains unclear whether Ronaldo intends to return to the national team or if coach Jorge Jesus will select him again.
body: Cristiano Ronaldo successfully fought to reduce his punishment for walking out on a Portugal training camp, after publicly saying his sanction should be imposed “without mitigating circumstances”.

Ronaldo said in a lengthy statement on social media after he left the camp in Denmark last month that he should be punished as the Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) saw fit and that his role as captain constituted “an aggravating factor”.

However, during the disciplinary council’s inquiry the 41-year-old put forward several arguments for cutting his punishment, including his clean disciplinary record in recent seasons and his services to football.

Ronaldo received a 30-day suspension and €255 (£215) fine, and the document accompanying the ruling reveals he presented three arguments in mitigation: his disciplinary record this season and in the previous three seasons, his services to football including recognition for sporting merit, and his contribution to establishing the facts of the case.

To support these arguments, Ronaldo listed the club titles he has won and his achievements with the national team: the 2016 European Championship and two Nations League titles. His individual awards were also highlighted, including the fact that the Al-Nassr forward has won the Ballon d’Or five times. Beyond his achievements on the pitch, he mentioned the honours he had received from senior state officials.

The decision-makers accepted Ronaldo’s arguments concerning his achievements and services to the country, using them to halve his suspension and fine. The punishment was then halved again because Ronaldo had accepted responsibility for his actions.

Ronaldo’s suspension will be served in a period during which there are no international matches. It is unclear whether he intends to return to the national team – or whether the coach, Jorge Jesus, will select him again.

The account of events provides a clearer picture of the circumstances surrounding Ronaldo’s departure from the training camp. After head coach Jesus held a press conference in which he reiterated that he was in charge of the team and that no player would influence his selection decisions, Ronaldo requested a vehicle from the FPF and set off for Copenhagen airport.
During the journey, he called the Portuguese federation’s president, Pedro Proença, and told him he was “not in the right frame of mind” to remain with the team.

“The defendant [Ronaldo] did not inform or provide prior justification to the federation or the men’s national team officials regarding his intention to leave the stadium and the training camp,” the ruling states. It says that between 30 September and 4 October, Ronaldo missed more than 30 team activities, including travel, training sessions and meals.

The federation says that Ronaldo’s promise on social media, after leaving the training camp, to tell his fans “the whole truth” brought further negative attention to the incident: “Given his prominence as a public figure on a global scale, the defendant could not have been unaware that his conduct, in the circumstances in which it occurred, would be subject to intense media scrutiny, as indeed it was.”

Ronaldo was therefore “expected to exercise particular caution in choosing the timing and manner in which he expressed his dissatisfaction with the manager’s decisions and conduct”. Instead, the player “further fuelled speculation and public curiosity by posting on Instagram on the very day he left Copenhagen, announcing that, ‘in due course’, he would tell ‘all Portuguese people the truth about the reasons that led to his departure from the men’s senior national team’,” the inquiry concluded.
Portugal are scheduled to play Denmark again in their next game on 14 November in Braga.

articles.headline: "I want room to make a wrong turn": Following Samson dev's bankruptcy, its founder is considering how AI might factor into new studio plans
keyFacts: Swedish developer Liquid Swords has filed for bankruptcy less than a year after releasing its debut game, Samson.
Founder Christofer Sundberg announced plans to form a new studio with a small team, low costs, and a sustainable business model.
Sundberg stated that generative AI may be used for prototyping and testing, but not to replace human roles.
body: Over the weekend, Swedish reports revealed that Samson studio Liquid Swords have gone bankrupt less than a year after releasing their debut crimebrawler. Founder and former Just Cause lead Christofer Sundberg subsequently confirmed that Liquid Swords are headed for closure. However, he was also quick to make clear that he won't be disappearing from game development, announcing plans to form a new studio that he's now offered a bit more insight on.

"I’ll be back at it again soon and will share more about my plans for a new studio," Sundberg wrote as part of his LinkedIn post about Liquid Swords' impending closure. "It will be built with the current market in mind, with a solid foundation and business decisions that give the games and the people making them room to succeed. The lessons from Liquid Swords will be part of how I build it.I still love making games."

While stressing that nothing's in place as of right now, the dev offered a more detailed picture of the thoughts he's had thus far in terms of how this new studio might approach development and avoid the same pitfalls as Liquid Swords in a chat with PC Gamer.

"A small, experienced team, low running costs and a game we can afford to finish without needing every sales forecast to come true," is what Sundberg said he envisions, adding that having "room to make a wrong turn, fix it, and keep going without putting the whole company at risk" is key. Generative AI also factors into that equation, with the developer outlining that he sees it as being used "to help with prototyping, repetitive production tasks and testing".

"We're not looking to replace roles with AI or treating it as a way to save money (or make money quickly), because AI is bloody expensive too," he expanded. "And cutting corners in game development has a habit of coming back to bite you in the ass." Sundberg went on to specify that he's "positive about these tools", but doesn't believe simply declaring you're 'AI-first' is a viable production plan or business strategy. "You need people who understand the work well enough to know when AI helps and when to switch it off," he added. "I'd like [people in the industry] to talk more openly about that."

When myself and Julian played Samson earlier this year, I ran particularly badly afoul of the serious bugs which plagued the PC version early doors. Julian was luckier in that regard, and we both came to appreciate the distinct character offered by its debt-paying central loop, while acknowledging that both the bugs and the clear limitations the game had been built under meant that core idea didn't achieve its full potential. Here's hoping all of the developers who made it end up landing on their feet and aren't left with uncertain futures while their former boss happily goes about his next chapter.

articles.headline: NY congressional nominee Brad Lander says he was detained by the IDF in the West Bank
keyFacts: New York congressional nominee Brad Lander stated on social media that he was detained by the Israeli Defense Forces while harvesting olives in the West Bank.
The human rights group Rabbis for Human Rights corroborated that Lander and 90 other volunteers were held by the IDF after the area was designated a closed military zone.
Lander has previously been an outspoken critic of Israel, having opposed unconditional military aid and accused the country of conducting a genocide in Gaza.
body: Lefty congressional nominee Brad Lander claimed Wednesday he was “detained” by the Israeli Defense Forces while working on an olive harvest in the West Bank.
“I’ve been detained by the IDF, along with a group of rabbis & volunteers,” Lander posted on X. “We were simply harvesting olives in a grove near Nehalim in the West Bank.”
It is unclear if Lander, who is vying for New York’s 10th Congressional District seat, was doing anything else besides olive harvesting.
“The occupation is a crime under international law. Harvesting olives isn’t a crime under any law I know,” he added.
Lander had bested outgoing Rep. Dan Goldman (D-NY) in their June primary, mounting a challenge against him from the left. Lander, who is Jewish, has been an outspoken critic of Israel.
During his primary against Goldman and his unsuccessful run for mayor last year, Lander made Israel a top issue.
The Dem candidate has opposed unconditional military aid to the Jewish state and accused it of carrying out a genocide in the Gaza Strip after the bloody Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack.

“I think — with deep sadness — that Israel’s conduct in Gaza meets the definition of genocide. But even if you don’t, it’s profoundly inconsistent with the Jewish value that every one of those Palestinian kids were created in the image of God, just like ours,” he posted on X in June.
Lander also contended that “Israel can’t be a genuine democracy while it’s occupying the West Bank & Gaza.”

Rabbis for Human Rights, an Israeli human rights group, corroborated Lander’s claim about being detained and said 90 other volunteers were held by the IDF as well, while harvesting olives in Nahalin, outside Bethlehem.
Authorities designated the area they were working in as a military zone closed for a full day, according to the group.
Officials then checked the group for identification, despite the group’s leaders offering to leave voluntarily, according to Rabbis for Human Rights’ version of events.

“We came to accompany farmers to land they have not been able to reach in three years, and after two hours of quiet harvesting, large forces arrived and closed the area,” Acting executive director for Rabbis for Human Rights, Anton Goodman, said in a statement.
“No one could have known about this order in advance. Instead of protecting people working their own land, the army is removing them from it, and detaining those who came to stand beside them.”
Lander previously described his venture to the West Bank as a mission to help Palestinians with their harvest and to put the spotlight on conditions there.

Other lefty pols have had similar run-ins with Israeli authorities. In July, for example, Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) said he and his group were detained by the Israelis for over an hour while in the Palestinian village of Khirbet Zanuta during a tour.

articles.headline: I've played 2 of Dawn of War 4's campaigns, and they're everything I hoped they'd be
keyFacts: The reviewer played two campaigns for Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 featuring the orks and the Adeptus Mechanicus.
The ork campaign focuses on a fast-paced rivalry and race between two opposing ork factions on the world of Kronos.
The Adeptus Mechanicus campaign offers a slower, high-tech playstyle centered around the Noosphere Network and fighting necrons.
body: An RTS is only as good as its campaign. Sure, it's the competitive multiplayer side of things that gives these games their long tail—StarCraft 2 has been the dominant RTS for 16 years for this very reason—but the bulk of initial players will first be seduced by the promise of a killer singleplayer romp. In this regard, Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4 has the juice.

I've had a couple of weeks to play around with two of the four campaigns—orks and Adeptus Mechanicus—along with the shorter, two-mission prologue featuring the Astra Militarum, and I've been able to set aside my fear that we'd be getting a repeat of Dawn of War 3's issues. Folks, I am loving these campaigns.
Lads, lads lads

Out of the prologue, I signed up with the orks. The greenskins are a good first pick, not just because this campaign comes first in the chronology, but because it's the most straightforward faction. Their units and buildings are the cheapest in the game, and it only takes a few minutes to recruit a basic army right out of the gate. If you just want to smash shit up, the orks are your guys.

This is not to say that you'll be steamrolling everything. You can lose that army even quicker than you recruited it if you just charge in blind. Orks might not be the brightest xenos in the universe, but their ruthlessness and rage is tempered by low cunning—something the campaign narrative leans into.

If you want to make the most out of your green tide of devastation, you'll want to do a bit of recon, figuring out what toys your opponents are playing with. This won't just determine the units you should recruit, but the wargear upgrades you give them as well. Like the tabletop game, you're given a lot of versatility, which includes being able to switch up the weapons on individual units, which in turn lets you handle specific threats more effectively.

The ork campaign is a fun one, full of large green idiots posturing, backstabbing and getting all charged up about the prospect of squashing humies. You'll start as the boss of a local band of angry lads, but then spacefaring orks fall from the sky, and their boss (a familiar face for Dawn of War vets) quickly decides the world of Kronos is his—the native orks aren't really OK with that.

So a lot of this campaign is focused on this competition between the two groups. A particularly great mission sees you competing in a race with this ork interloper. The first side to destroy the Adeptus Mechanicus base wins the race and gets to be the big boss (not that orks are sportsmanlike or tend to honour deals).
Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

The armies are separated and must push up their respective paths, with the UI showing who's winning. It's a brilliantly designed map, with a slight MOBA vibe because of its lane setup, but also featuring some spacious areas for big fights and base building, lots of chokepoints, and some elevated positions that you'll need your Stormboyz to overcome. Across most of it, you're separated from the other orks, but you can still see them pushing their way up the map, which I found even more effective than the UI when it came to lighting a fire under my arse. At the top and bottom of the map, however, the two sides are linked, which inspires a bunch of sneaky backstabbing.

Your opponent starts sending small forces to harass your base, keeping you on your toes, and then your main armies clash at the top of the map, near the Adeptus Mechanicus base. I had a vast green horde and a respectable lead, but the tech priests were able to hold me off for a wee while, giving my opponent time to catch up. It was the best way to end the mission: a climactic battle where I was squished between humans and enemy orks. When the last building crumbled, most of my army was gone, but it didn't matter—I'd won the challenge.

After the race, you pick a side—the local boyz or the invaders—for the rest of the campaign. Some of the maps and objectives are shared between the two paths, but you'll also encounter unique missions, story moments and, of course, you'll have very different commander units to play around with. It's a smart way to solve the one-and-done nature of RTS campaigns—you'll need to play twice to experience everything. And even within the same path, you're occasionally forced to make certain decisions that will affect future missions.

As a tabletop boy, I feel pretty well taken care of in DoW4. Not being a methodical turn-based romp, it's naturally going to feel different, but it's undeniably authentic. There's the adaptation of the wargear system that I mentioned above, of course, but things like stratagems and command points also make their way over from the tabletop version.

Command points can be earned by fighting and taking over capture points, which can then be spent on activating powerful abilities, the aforementioned stratagems. They've helped me turn the tide of battle more than a few times. They're all great. Whether I'm summoning some explosive squigs, calling down a random unit—which naturally obliterates anything in the landing zone—or psychically buffing my entire army by calling a WAAAGH!, stratagems always promise a good time, and they live up to it.

The orks are also just a delight to watch, with their exaggerated animations and colourful model design, flawlessly evoking the tabletop game. Zooming in and watching a melee scrum play out is well worth the sacrifice of battlefield visibility, especially with the synced up animations. King Art has expanded this system, so it doesn't just sync up units when there's a kill.

Now, it doesn't always work as advertised. I often see units flailing around and not hitting anything, but I've also witnessed plenty of flashy duels playing out. Broadly, DoW4's scraps have a high level of physicality, with clashes between forces feeling tangible and tactile. And with a couple of months between now and launch, hopefully it will look even better in the finished build.
Heavy metal

After I finished up with my ork besties, the Adeptus Mechanicus campaign was a big change of pace. This is the first time these nerds have featured in Dawn of War, but good things come to those who wait—whether it's Guinness or tech priests. It's a fun tonal shift from the brutality of the green lads, with the Adeptus Mechanicus being the scalpel to the ork's blunt instrument.

The structure of the Adeptus Mechanicus campaign is similar to its ork counterpart, in that there's a big rivalry that allows you, after a certain point, to pick one of two paths with different commanders. The ork and Adeptus Mechanicus campaigns, and their respective paths, still feel suitably different, however, with bespoke missions and distinct characters giving each a powerful flavour all their own.

Technoarchaeology and immortal machines—that's what you're getting into with the Adeptus Mechanicus. The Imperium's dogmatic tinkerers make for a high-tech, precise army as they attempt to thwart the awakened necron forces on Kronos. Like the ork campaign, it's blessed with lots of variety, boasting plenty of novel missions and deftly avoiding too much repetition.

The tech priests are a ranged powerhouse, certainly compared to the orks, but right from the get-go you'll get access to stealthy melee units that do a great job of locking down ranged enemies or slaughtering foes who are hunkering down behind cover.

Oh yeah, cover is back! Thank the Emperor. Cover was a big part of the first two games, but it got sidelined in DoW3. Relic's third game did technically have a cover system, with small areas that you could capture, after which a temporary shield would offer units inside a bit of protection, but it was a poor system. These locations were few and far between, often placed in areas where they weren't really needed, and the nature of the missions—where you rarely stay in one place for long—rendered them largely useless.

DoW4's approach should keep everyone pretty happy. Every map features barricades, plonked down in sensible spots, and during the more scripted campaign missions they are almost always a sign that an enemy army is going to be charging towards you. They are vulnerable to melee units and flanking attacks, but will keep your ranged units alive for longer.

Orks can actually construct their own barricades, which can be erected anywhere.The Adeptus Mechanicus, meanwhile, aren't left out in the cold. They're able to construct a different kind of cover: Emanatus Field Generators. As you'd expect from a technologically advanced faction with a ranged focus, these are fancier than the basic cover. They absorb melee damage and protect units garrisoned inside them from ranged attacks, and the coverage is 360 degrees, too, rather than being directional.

I got so much use out of the various types of cover, and they can dramatically change the flow of battle and give important roles to specific units. But cover doesn't make units invincible, and it can be destroyed, so there are plenty of ways to deal with protected enemies.

Grenades are handy, of course, and so are fast melee units if you're dealing with barricades. The Adeptus Mechanicus Sicarian Ruststalker or the ork Squighog Boyz can quickly get behind cover and then lock the ranged unit into a fight, completely defanging them and making them vulnerable once more.

All this is to say: cover has a huge impact, both when you're facing it and using it. But it's not the only defensive measure. The Adeptus Mechanicus also has access to a rather impressive bit of tech known as the Void Shield. This bad boy can protect your base from anyone outside the shield, as it's not possible for enemies to shoot through it. They must walk into your base to do damage, at which point they can be surrounded and taken out.

While DoW4 is a pretty fast-paced game, the Adeptus Mechanicus are a touch slower and more deliberate than the orks. While the latter can rapidly plonk down some buildings anywhere on the map and spit out an army, the tech priests take a little longer to get going—but that's not a disadvantage.

See, the Adeptus Mechanicus warmachine is fuelled by the Noosphere Network, a system that links up the faction's buildings, turrets and field generators, and confers a multitude of benefits, improving the efficiency of both their bases and armies. Through relays you can spread the network across the entire map, so distant outposts or defended positions can benefit from the efficiency boost. But these relays are vulnerable, so the bigger the network, the more you need to invest time and resources defending it.

But expand it you must—because the larger the network, the more powerful it becomes, eventually netting you fancy end-game units, research and upgrade options. It's a lovely bit of friction: to become stronger, you must also make yourself a bit more vulnerable. If the enemy takes out a critical relay, you could be screwed.

There's more to consider in an Adeptus Mechanicus playthrough, then, but damn do they have some fun toys to play with—as you'd expect from 40k's most overzealous gearheads. The Knight is a highlight of course—a gargantuan behemoth that towers over the battlefield—and the faction boasts some powerful stratagems, including one that can wipe out an entire enemy force if you time it just right. It's beautiful stuff.
Room for everyone

As a fan of Iron Harvest, which took a lot of cues from original Dawn of War developer Relic, I expected to enjoy DoW4. But a good RTS campaign is not guaranteed, even when it's coming from a proven studio—just look at the last game, which almost killed off the whole series. From what I've played so far, however, I think King Art is onto a winner here.

OK, now it's time to address the elephant in the room: Total War 40k. It's been suggested that Creative Assembly's take on Warhammer 40k will steal DoW4's thunder. I don't see it. First of all, DoW4 is right around the corner, while Total War 40k doesn't even have a release date. They're also just completely different kinds of strategy games.

DoW4 is a classic, pure RTS with a series of mostly linear campaigns and an emphasis on storytelling. It's a smaller scale romp, and probably a bit tighter and tidier as a result. Total War 40k, like all Total Wars, is more like a grand strategy game with real-time tactical pitched battles. There's no base building, the maps are mostly open and the campaigns will be sandboxes.

They are completely different experiences, and there's room for everyone. Indeed, I feel pretty damn lucky to have a new Dawn of War and a new Total War to look forward to—it's a good thing. Take it from someone who's played both. So there's never been a better time to be a 40k fan—that said, between Dark Heresy, Dawn of War 4, Total War 40k and the new battleforce boxes Games Workshop just unveiled, I'm about to be a broke 40k fan.

Fraser is the UK online editor and has actually met The Internet in person. With over a decade of experience, he's been around the block a few times, serving as a freelancer, news editor and prolific reviewer. Strategy games have been a 30-year-long obsession, from tiny RTSs to sprawling political sims, and he never turns down the chance to rave about Total War or Crusader Kings. He's also been known to set up shop in the latest MMO and likes to wind down with an endlessly deep, systemic RPG. These days, when he's not editing, he can usually be found writing features that are 1,000 words too long or talking about his dog.

articles.headline: What to do if you feel so, so angry at the state of the world
keyFacts: Buddhist teacher Lama Rod Owens states that anger is physical tension and acts as energy pointing to a deeper heartbrokenness.
Rabbi Nate DeGroot notes that Jewish tradition compares anger to a passing moment that is superseded by enduring compassion.
Executive director Najeeba Syeed explains that Islamic tradition views anger as a tool to recognize problems, while justice requires connection and love.
body: Are you mad about everything?

Another needless, endless war. Rising living costs and gas prices. The fact that the richest 1 percent of Americans own more than the bottom 90 percent combined, or the straight-up corruption happening in the White House. As the old saying goes, if you’re not mad, you’re not paying attention.
But what does spirituality teach us about how to respond to our anger? Is it wise to try to let it go? Should we practice imagining clouds floating gently by and take a deep breath?

I don’t think so. For one, it’s not that simple! There’s way too much happening inside my heart when I’m pissed off to pretend that I’m full of calm and kindness. Plus, this kind of spiritual bypassing is as insulting as it is ineffective. When we try to force a feeling, we fundamentally misunderstand the gift that anger has to give us: a deeper insight into our pain and a genuine compassion that enables wise action for justice.

That said, I don’t want to walk around like a fire-breathing dragon or endlessly stew in my resentment either. So I reached out to some trustworthy religious voices to see what spiritual traditions can teach us about effective responses to our rage — and how it can give us insight without overwhelming us.
Underneath your anger is a broken heart

Lama Rod Owens is a Buddhist teacher in Atlanta and the author of Love and Rage: The Path of Liberation Through Anger . The first thing he tells me is that we have to acknowledge our anger. “A lot of us actually don’t know what anger feels like. We’re just reacting to it,” he says. And that rings true. I’m still learning to notice the physical signs of rage: My head gets hot; my stomach tight; my throat fills with the scream that I’m only just able to contain.

That physicality is central to Owens’s definition of anger: The mental and physical tension out of which aggression arises. And that aggressive response is what gets me into trouble — when I snap at my husband or give demon eyes at those who surely have headphones but are choosing not to use them. If I’m not careful, I won’t even notice how rageful I am until my simmering pot of fury suddenly comes to a boil.

Noticing that tension can be tricky, Owens says, because “a lot of people get gaslit around their anger, particularly women and femme folks.” It can be radical to simply admit that anger is arising in you. Owens is very careful with language here. Instead of saying that we are angry, he encourages us to say that we feel angry. “I know it’s very nuanced,” he explains, “but when people start thinking about an experience rather than being something, it really opens up space.”
And that space gives us what we need to take the next step. Which, surely, is to move past our anger?

No, he argues. The path of liberation is through anger — not to “get over it.” Owens learned this through personal experience, as well as through the wisdom teachings of his Buddhist lineage. As a Black, queer man living in America, he’s had plenty to be angry about (while also having to navigate the harmful stereotype that as a Black man he’s inherently angry). But, he writes in his book, “I wasn’t pissed off because of racism or homophobia or something else. I was actually deeply, deeply hurt.” Through disciplined meditation, Owens realized that his anger was a secondary emotion. Meaning, there was a primary experience that sat underneath the anger. And that primary experience was pain and sadness and a deeper sense of heartbrokenness.
“It’s like you’re not just angry, experiencing anger about the world. You’re hurt by the world, you’re saddened by the world, you’re grieving the world,” he says.

Learning to sit with that anger shifted things over time. As Owens practiced noticing and naming his rage instead of trying to push it away or acting out in aggression, he found a way to be with it instead.

His Buddhist lineage taught him to think of anger simply as energy. And like any energy, he learned to experience it rather than to react to it: “In Buddhism, we would consider the essence [of anger] to be empty…it’s just energy that can be shaped or misunderstood by consciousness.”
To be clear, he says, “It’s not like the anger disappeared,” but rather that Owens experienced enough space around the anger that allowed him to name the heartbreak that was underneath it.
And once he could do that, he noticed a completely different feeling flooding in.
Moving through anger to tender compassion

Nate DeGroot has seen the same connection. DeGroot is a rabbi based in Detroit and the director of the Shalom Center. In his Jewish tradition, anger isn’t just something only humans experience — God gets angry, too. Think of the flood sent to punish humankind that Noah avoids by building the ark, for example. But, DeGroot explains, God’s anger only lasts a moment.

In fact, in Jewish tradition, the Talmud records people questioning exactly how long God’s anger lasts — with some claiming that it remains only for a 15,888th of an hour (which comes to just under half a second), and others saying God’s wrath lasts as long as it takes to say the word “moment” in Hebrew, a word with two syllables. Either way, it only lasts a short while, because a deeper, more enduring compassion quickly emanates from God’s being.

As the parent of two small kids, DeGroot empathizes with both God’s anger — and the love that supersedes it. When his kids mess around, he says, “I’m frustrated!…why did they fling the blue toothpaste on the white shade in the bathroom and now it’s forever stained? I’ve got to bring the rug into the rug cleaner for the fifth time in two years because they peed on it in the middle of the night!” he says, laughing. But those temporary flares of frustration sit within a wider circle of parental care. “I really relate to… this notion of the moment of anger [being] situated within a broader, more expansive, everlasting love,” he tells me.

Once we’ve properly noticed our anger and named the heartbreak it masks, what will (hopefully!) follow is waves of compassion for ourselves and everyone else that is hurting. And it is from that place that you can actually take action.
From compassion comes a community for justice

Najeeba Syeed is the executive director of Interfaith at Augsburg in Minneapolis and has a long history of doing conflict resolution work. She explains that in Islam, too, the Prophet Muhammad experiences anger. Early in his mission as he travels from one place to another, he’s stoned by angry villagers who reject him. “He was given a choice,” she tells Vox. “Should the divine force go and destroy this community, or should this community have reprieve for what they’ve done?”

The Prophet Muhammad chooses forgiveness over revenge. But there’s both spiritual wisdom and strategy at play in that choice: Anger can separate us from the very people we need to be connected to when seeking justice, Syeed says. “It makes us incapable of seeing the experience of others,” she says. And it is precisely the experience of other people we need to be aware of when building coalitions that will be able to solve the problems that make us angry. Inequality and corruption and rising health care costs are not going to change if we remain atomized and mad. We have to work together.

“Okay, you’re angry,” Syeed affirms, “But who is the you? Who is in the collective? Who is impacted? If we don’t have a larger identity than our political affiliation — by that I mean the neighborliness , some sense of community that transcends that identitarian political affiliation alone — then we may actually destroy ourselves in the process.”
“If you [take action] by yourself, is it really going to change at the social level?” she asks. “You still have to be able to build allies, and you still have to be able to build connection.”

That’s what the Prophet Muhammad was doing in exhibiting restraint with the angry villagers. In leaving them unpunished, he was later able to build an alliance with them in his campaign to spread his message through the region.

In the Muslim tradition, a judge is forbidden from making a ruling when angry because it is understood that justice cannot come from rage. Anger helps us cut through distractions and focus on the work that needs to be done — but that work for justice must come from a deeper place of love.

So, how should we think of anger? Not as something to indulge — but nor should we try to avoid it. Anger is like an alarm bell, telling us something is wrong. When we notice it arising, we must inspect the heartbreak that lies underneath and allow for our innate compassion to emerge. And then guided by that love — and a dash of strategy — we can decide how to act.

And act we should! Syeed shares a popular saying in the Islamic world: One must tie their own camel. It means that we humans have to intervene in the world; it isn’t just up to the divine to act for us. So: Have hard conversations guided by your morals! Vote in the midterms and in local elections! Call your electeds! Organize your neighbors and your workplace ! But do it out of that deeper compassion that guides wise decision-making.

articles.headline: Exclusive: ServiceNow and Nvidia launch Arc, a new AI agent for enterprise
keyFacts: Software company ServiceNow and Nvidia launched Arc, an enterprise AI agent built for Nvidia RTX Spark devices, which is generally available now.
ServiceNow and Nvidia stated that Arc handles everyday productivity tasks locally while building memory and skills over time to improve its performance.
ServiceNow and Nvidia stated that Arc features a multi-level security framework with hardware-level controls designed to prevent breaches and enforce company policies.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- Arc, originally announced in May, is now generally available.
- The agent is built for Nvidia’s new RTX Spark devices.
- Multi-level security infrastructure around Arc aims to give businesses peace of mind.

One of the main roadblocks to adopting more autonomous AI systems for companies is adequate security controls, especially after a summer of agent-led breaches. Software company ServiceNow has partnered with Nvidia to address that need by combining AI capabilities with security-first guardrails.

Arc, which ServiceNow and Nvidia call “a personal long-running AI agent that can take on everyday work,” is generally available as of Wednesday. The companies originally released the idea for the agent back in May. Arc is available now on Mac, but Windows support is still on the way.
What Arc can do

Like many agents built for enterprise use, Arc is designed for daily tasks that rely on productivity tools such as email and Microsoft Teams. Designed to run efficiently on Nvidia’s new RTX Spark devices, it can run locally on an employee’s desktop or within Nvidia OpenShell on its own device. Similar to other agents that work off of accumulated context, ServiceNow and Nvidia said Arc builds memory and skills over time so that its performance continually improves.
More from ZDNET

The companies also said Arc is efficient, handing more complex tasks off to frontier models only when necessary and keeping data as local as possible otherwise. ServiceNow and Nvidia also said that Arc “proactively surfaces work and action items” by scanning an employee’s inbox and meeting notes.

But more than any new or highly competitive capabilities overall, what sets Arc apart, according to the companies, is the multi-level security framework surrounding it. ServiceNow and Nvidia said their approach offers more reliable security by “moving enforcement beyond the software layer into the runtime and hardware layers.”
Essentially, while the Arc agent is working on tasks, ServiceNow’s Super Intelligence Control Tower enforces company policies, while Nvidia OpenShell restricts the agent’s behavior where necessary.

“IT defines policies in the Super Intelligence Control Tower and NVIDIA OpenShell can be directed to enforce them at runtime,” the announcement explained. “Users obtain granular control over which systems AI agents can access, APIs they can call, and data they can read.”
AI Passport

AI Passport is another layer of agent security that the two companies announced last week. It holds an enterprise’s set of rules, which the Control Tower sets, about risk tolerance and the services Arc and other agents are allowed to access. That lets Nvidia’s features like OpenShell intervene efficiently if an AI agent takes action it’s not supposed to, the companies explained.

With the other pieces of ServiceNow and Nvidia’s security puzzle, AI Passport functions like a bridge between ServiceNow infrastructure and Nvidia’s checkpoints. The entire system is designed to continuously monitor an agent’s actions and permissions to prevent breaches, unsanctioned actions, and other fallout from using agents.

If the Control Tower tells OpenShell an agent’s passport has been revoked, OpenShell will keep the task the agent was trying to execute contained within a sandbox, where reviewers can audit it later. That interruption is also task-specific, meaning other, approved agent actions can continue without restarting.

“When a passport is revoked in the Super Intelligence Control Tower, Nvidia BlueField can enforce that revocation at machine speed before the AI agent can proceed,” the companies said. “This creates enforcement in silicon designed to prevent overrides from compromised software.”

articles.headline: Minecraft and Domino’s Team Up for Block-Shaped Pizza, In-Game Freebies
keyFacts: Domino's Pizza is partnering with Minecraft to offer block-shaped pizza and in-game rewards starting Monday.
Customers purchasing the Detroit-style pizza online receive a code for one of three in-game items for Minecraft Dungeons II.
Domino's stated that 20,000 free game downloads will be given away through a lottery for customers who submit their proof of purchase.
body: The computer game Minecraft offers plenty of in-game food, from steak and cake to, uh, rotten flesh. Now, a popular real-world food is being mixed with Minecraft.

Beginning on Monday, Domino’s Pizza will offer Minecraft-themed tie-ins, including in-game extras, when customers buy “the Domino,” a recently launched Detroit-style pizza for one. The pizza is cut into two pieces to resemble Minecraft blocks, in connection with the new game Minecraft Dungeons II, a spin-off of the 2020 game Minecraft Dungeons.
Minecraft Dungeons II came out Sept. 29 for PC, Xbox Series X and S, PlayStation 5, Nintendo Switch and Switch 2.
More from CNET

As part of the Minecraft collab, the rectangular Detroit-style Domino pizza will come in one of six game-related boxes, each featuring a different Minecraft Dungeons II character: the classic Creeper, Corrupted Creeper, Zombie, Pig, Prime Enchanter and the main protagonist, Valorie.
When you buy the pizza online, you can unlock a code for one of three randomly awarded in-game items to use in Minecraft Dungeons II: a Domino’s skin, a Slice Slayer Cape, and a Cheesy Cube pet.

Between Monday and Nov. 4, customers have a chance to win a free download of the game (for PC and Xbox only), normally priced at $30. Domino’s says 20,000 downloads will be given away. To enter the lottery, after purchasing “the Domino,” submit your proof of purchase on its dedicated web page.

articles.headline: Russia frees retired American teacher as Trump envoy meets with Putin
keyFacts: Russia released retired American teacher Stephen Hubbard, who was detained in Ukraine in 2022, as a goodwill gesture.
U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg to hold peace talks.
President Donald Trump stated that Hubbard is returning home and that the U.S. gave nothing in return.
body: Russia has released retired American teacher Stephen Hubbard, 74, the latest sign of warmer ties between the two countries as Washington pressures Kyiv to agree to a deal to end Moscow’s war.

U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff lauded President Vladimir Putin for the release of Hubbard as he held peace talks with the Russian leader early Wednesday in St. Petersburg. “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir,” Witkoff said.

The U.S. has courted the Kremlin for weeks, and the release of Hubbard — a Michigan native detained in Ukraine in 2022 — will give President Donald Trump a victory to tout after backlash at home and abroad for his tilt away from Kyiv in the conflict.

Trump hailed the news. “Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family. The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return — an unprecedented situation for Russia,” he said in a post on Truth Social.

Trump said that he had directly asked Putin in a phone call last week to release Hubbard, who was being held on charges he denies of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine. He was the last American designated as wrongfully detained in Russia by the State Department.
The Kremlin said the move was a goodwill gesture.

Hubbard’s family thanked “President Trump and his team for opening the dialog with Russia which led to this joyful day. Our family can attest that there are wonderful blessings to be found along the hard road to peace.”

In video from Russian state news agency Ria, Hubbard can be seen wearing a green jacket and smiling. “Thank you very much for all your efforts,” the freed American tells Witkoff as they shake hands. Putin sent Hubbard “blessings,” Witkoff tells him, adding “from today, it’s a new life.”
U.S. peace push

The meeting between Putin and Witkoff, which Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner was expected to join virtually, came after the American negotiators met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European leaders in the Norwegian capital, Oslo.
Ukraine brought forward new ideas and proposals at those talks, a U.S. official told NBC News, adding that “meaningful progress” was made as the Trump administration intensifies its peace push.

Diplomacy has made little headway for months, and this renewed American effort has drawn widespread criticism as Trump announced a series of moves to bolster Russia while Ukraine accused the U.S. of withdrawing crucial support.

“We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Tuesday, intensifying a pressure campaign that has fueled concern the U.S. is no longer committed to Kyiv’s defense against the Russian invasion.
“We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss,” Trump said.

Witkoff told Putin on Wednesday that “groundwork” had been laid for ending the fighting, and that he had brought documents outlining approaches to a possible deal. He also said he hoped that the Russian leader would consider resuming trilateral talks.
Zelenskyy said that a potential trilateral leaders’ meeting was “one of the important ideas” raised in Oslo after Tuesday’s talks, which also included the leaders of Norway and Finland.

Putin has so far insisted any meeting with Zelenskyy could only happen once a deal is finalized and take place in Moscow, a nonstarter for Ukraine. The Kremlin has also shown little sign of shifting from its hard-line demands, which include seizing Ukraine’s entire eastern Donbas region.

Trump signed a diesel deal with Russia earlier this month and waived new sanctions on Moscow, drawing bipartisan criticism. He claimed Wednesday that negotiations to free Hubbard “would have come to a complete and total halt” if he hadn’t waived the sanctions.

Kyiv, meanwhile, said it received no advance warning about at least three major Russian attacks and that restrictions on Elon Musk’s Starshield satellite service continue to hamper its aerial defenses and battlefield operations.
After the talks with Witkoff on Tuesday, Zelenskyy told reporters the recent issues with intelligence sharing had been resolved.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the talks in Oslo “positive,” but said “nothing unexpected” came out of them.

Rubio once again denied that the White House was behind any slowdown to Ukraine’s use of the internet service, saying this was an issue for Musk and SpaceX. Musk himself said last week any decision was down to Trump.
Deadly Russian attacks continued to hit Ukraine, meanwhile, with at least nine civilians killed across the country Wednesday as Moscow ramps up its strikes on energy infrastructure ahead of winter.
Authorities in Russia’s border Bryansk region said Wednesday that one person was killed in a Ukrainian strike.
